items.stem: Grace stayed overnight at Kwame's hotel in Lima. A large sign at the entrance, which Grace read before paying, excluded liability. Grace's property was later damaged through Kwame's staff's negligence. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: Incorporation of terms by notice. A term must be incorporated before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies incorporation of terms by notice. 1 mark: states the rule correctly, e.g. a term must be incorporated before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking). [2]

items.stem: Ethan stayed overnight at Grace's cloakroom in Mumbai. A sign excluding liability was displayed only inside, where Ethan saw it after paying. Ethan's property was later damaged through Grace's staff's negligence. Advise Ethan whether the exclusion term is part of the contract.
items.answer: Law: a term must be incorporated before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking); reasonable notice is required for unsigned terms (Parker v SE Railway); onerous terms require greater notice (Interfoto); even if incorporated, the term must satisfy statutory controls. Application: the notice here was not incorporated because notice came after the contract (Olley; Thornton). Conclusion: The term was not incorporated because notice came after the contract (Olley; Thornton).
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: identifies incorporation of terms by notice; accurate statement of the law, e.g. a term must be incorporated before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking); reasonable notice is required for unsigned terms (Parker v SE Railway); onerous terms require greater notice (Interfoto); even if incorporated, the term must satisfy statutory controls. AO2 Application [1]: applies the rules to the facts, e.g. the notice here was not incorporated because notice came after the contract (Olley; Thornton). items.stem: Explain three factors the courts consider when deciding whether a statement is a term or a representation.
items.answer: The importance of the statement to the claimant (Bannerman v White); the time between the statement and the contract (Routledge v McKay); whether the statement was put in writing; and the relative knowledge or expertise of the parties (Oscar Chess v Williams; Dick Bentley).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor with case, up to 3. [3]

items.stem: Lucas bought a used car from Diego, who is a car dealer. Before the sale Diego said that the used car had done only 30 000 miles. This was untrue. The written contract did not mention the statement. Advise Lucas whether the statement is a term of the contract. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion. Comment on any uncertainty in the law.
items.answer: Law: factors: importance (Bannerman v White), timing (Routledge v McKay), written form, special knowledge (Oscar Chess; Dick Bentley); if a term, Lucas can sue for breach of contract; if a representation, for misrepresentation. Application: Diego is a car dealer; Diego is an expert, so the statement is likely to be a term (Dick Bentley v Harold Smith); the statement that the used car had done only 30 000 miles was important to Lucas, but was not included in the written contract. Conclusion: Diego is an expert, so the statement is likely to be a term (Dick Bentley v Harold Smith).

items.stem: Lina Ltd, a printing company, bought printing ink from Kenji Ltd under Kenji Ltd's standard terms, which limited liability to the price paid ($8 000). The printing ink were defective, causing Lina Ltd a loss of $150 000. Advise Lina Ltd whether the limitation clause is effective. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: UCTA 1977 applies to business contracts; s3/s6 make such clauses subject to reasonableness; s11 and Schedule 2: bargaining power, insurance, knowledge of the term, industry practice; George Mitchell v Finney Lock Seeds (1983): limitation unreasonable where seller could insure and usually paid out. Application: the clause was incorporated in Kenji Ltd's standard terms; limiting liability to $8 000 against a loss of $150 000 may be unreasonable; relevant: whether Kenji Ltd could insure, bargaining power and whether Lina Ltd could buy elsewhere. Conclusion: The clause may well fail the reasonableness test, in which case Lina Ltd can recover the full loss of $150 000.
